Posted July 5, 2002
MarijuanaNews Exclusive Report.
See

The British government's war on the sick and dying continued today in a Manchester courtroom. It would appear that they have lost the latest battle, as they are losing the war, but they are nonetheless trying to inflict as much pain on Colin Davies as possible.

Once again the court ordered that Colin be released, because his second arrest was unlawful, but the prosecutor appealed the court ruling at the last minute and there will be a new hearing on Tuesday. Until then Colin will remain locked-up without cannabis, or even proper conventional pain treatment.

However, the stakes for the police and the prosecution are escalating. Not only is there the prospect of a lawsuit over the police abuse of Colin in the courtroom on Wednesday, they are now may also be sued for unlawful arrest and unlawful detention.

Here is how the situation has been explained to me:

When Colin was arrested by the police on Monday, they found cannabis at his flat. He was arrested for simplepossession of cannabis -- not possession with intent to supply, even though they knew the quantity involved.

That last point is key.

On Tuesday, the police sought to have him held until a hearing on July 11th. He was kept in custody to be taken to court for breaking his bail conditions. The police clearly expected him to be remanded to prison just for that. But the Magistrates accepted Colin's legal team's argument that it was medical necessity that drove him to break his bail conditions, and refused to remand him for that. Remember, Colin has twice beaten distribution charges, when juries refused to convict him for supplying cannabis to the sick and dying.

That should have meant Colin's release, but the police decided to arrest him for possession with intent to supply, and kept him in custody for that.

British law says that, once you have been given bail for something, the police can only arrest you again -- if they have new evidence which they were not aware of when you are given bail, but the police knew what quantity was involved on Monday.

Having decided to only charge him with possession, they had no right to arrest him again and charge him with possession with intent to supply, just because it went wrong for them in court.

If Colin's arrest was unlawful, then his continued detention is unlawful. If his legal team succeeds again on Tuesday, then he will have a civil claim for damages for unlawful arrest and detention, not to mention for being beaten by the police in a courtroom full of witnesses.

Disgracefully, " Don't mention the war " seems to be precisely the policy in the UK media, which still have not reported anything about Colin's case. Even the Manchester Evening News, for which this is a local story, has not reported it, even though they did report his release on bail in May.

Another matter that I find both disturbing and puzzling is the lack of reaction from any of Britain's excellent anti-prohibitionist groups. Although the activists in the Stockport area and even further afield have been steadfast, they should have support from civil liberty and other reform groups.

The London Times did report today that next Wednesday the Home Secretary will confirm that cannabis is to be rescheduled, as expected, which will make possession a non-arrestable offense. That will make Colin's jailing for possession of medical cannabis even more absurd.

www.globalhempmuseum.nl
